catalog.name: Antarctic Data Layers
catalog.description:
Introduction

The Antarctic Digital Twins catalogue brings several complementary datasets into one map so that atmospheric conditions, ice-sheet change, solid-Earth response and sub-ice geology can be explored together. The collection includes observations and derived products as well as numerical-model output, so each layer should be interpreted using its own methods and uncertainty information.

Data layers provided

AntAir ICE — Antarctic air temperature

The air-temperature layer is a daily snapshot from AntAir ICE, a 1 km near-surface air-temperature dataset covering terrestrial Antarctica, ice shelves and seasonal sea ice from 2003 to 2021. It was developed by Eva Bendix Nielsen and colleagues from MODIS land- and ice-surface temperatures calibrated against Antarctic automatic weather stations.

Values are stored in tenths of a degree Celsius. For example, a value of -300 represents -30 ℃.

Explore the AntAir visualisation · Metadata record · Dataset · Nielsen et al. (2023) study · Processing code

P-SKRIPS — atmosphere, sea-ice and ocean modelling

The P-SKRIPS layers show daily mean 10 m wind and near-surface air temperature from a coupled regional model of the Ross Sea. P-SKRIPS links Polar WRF with the MITgcm ocean and sea-ice model and was developed to conserve heat and freshwater fluxes between the components.

Wind speed is calculated from the eastward and northward wind components. The wind-arrow layer shows direction and speed and can be placed over the wind-speed raster. The Celsius and kelvin layers show the same temperature field in different units.

Explore the P-SKRIPS visualisation · Metadata record · Malyarenko et al. (2023) model study · Model code · January experiment data

Ice-sheet and glacial-isostatic-adjustment modelling

The Lowry ice-sheet layer shows modelled ice thickness for a selected simulation and time slice. Click a point on the map to chart ice thickness through the available model time steps, with one line for each model run.

The GIA layers represent the response of the solid Earth to changing ice loads. The anomaly layer shows the modelled adjustment, while global bed topography shows the evolving bed for a named model run. These products are model results rather than direct measurements; record the run identifier and model time whenever results are exported or compared.

Ice-sheet and GIA metadata record · Related Lowry research: deglacial grounding-line retreat in the Ross Embayment, geologic controls on Ross Embayment ice-sheet sensitivity, and late-Holocene ocean-cavity and grounding-line change.

Ross Ice Shelf basement and sediment thickness

The Tankersley layer estimates the thickness of non-magnetic sedimentary cover above magnetic basement beneath the Ross Ice Shelf and Ross Embayment. The study used airborne magnetic observations with seismic and Operation IceBridge constraints. Because this is a geophysical interpretation, quantitative work should also use the source uncertainty grids and flight-line information.

Metadata record · Dataset · Tankersley et al. (2022) study · Reproducible workflow · PolarToolkit examples

Experimental 3D ice-thickness blocks

The 3D layer is a proof of concept derived from one ice-model thickness band. Values are rounded upward into 250 m classes and positioned on the ETOPO surface. The columns are illustrative and their tops do not represent a reconstructed physical ice surface.

How to use the layers

  • Add one or more layers and use each legend to interpret its units and range.
  • Overlay P-SKRIPS wind arrows on wind speed to view direction and magnitude together.
  • Use either the Celsius or kelvin P-SKRIPS temperature layer; they display the same model field.
  • Click the Lowry ice-sheet layer to inspect modelled ice-thickness change through time and across runs.
  • Use layer names, run identifiers and dates when saving screenshots or reporting results.

Model and data limitations

  1. The catalogue combines observations, statistically derived datasets and model simulations. These products do not have the same evidential status or uncertainty.
  2. AntAir ICE depends on usable MODIS scenes and calibration against a sparse weather-station network. Cloud cover, season, surface type and location affect data availability and accuracy.
  3. P-SKRIPS represents a specific coupled-model setup. The published validation focused on one-month summer and winter experiments designed to test heat- and mass-flux conservation, not to establish a long-term observational climatology.
  4. The ice-sheet and GIA layers depend on model forcing, Earth rheology, parameter choices, initial conditions and the selected time slice. Compare multiple runs before treating a result as a preferred reconstruction.
  5. The Tankersley layer maps a geophysical interpretation of basement and sediment thickness, not directly sampled geology.
  6. The experimental 3D blocks are for visual exploration only and should not be used for quantitative reconstruction.

Data access, licensing and citation

Use the linked dataset repositories and metadata records to obtain the original files, licence terms and preferred citations. Cite both the relevant dataset and study when publishing analysis based on these layers.

Contacts

AntAir ICE: Eva Bendix Nielsen, eva.nielsen@pg.canterbury.ac.nz; Marwan Katurji, marwan.katurji@canterbury.ac.nz.

P-SKRIPS: Alena Malyarenko, alena.malyarenko@niwa.co.nz; Alexandra Gossart, alexandra.gossart@vuw.ac.nz.

For the Lowry and Tankersley products, use the current contact details in the linked metadata records and repositories.

Disclaimer

The layers are provided for scientific exploration and informational use. They are supplied "as is" without warranty regarding accuracy, completeness or fitness for a particular purpose. Consult the original data, metadata, uncertainty products and publications before quantitative, operational or safety-critical use.

members.name: Antarctic Air Temperature 2005-07-01
members.description: Daily near-surface air temperature from AntAir ICE for 1 July 2005. Values are stored in tenths of a degree Celsius, so -300 on the legend represents -30 ℃. The legend runs from -900 to 0. Please click the parent 'Antarctic Data Layers' folder for dataset methods, limitations, access and citation details.

members.name: GIA Anomaly
members.description: Glacial isostatic adjustment anomaly in metres. GIA is the slow deformation of the solid Earth as it responds to changes in ice load. The legend uses 200 m bands from below -800 m to above 800 m. This is model output rather than a direct measurement. Please click the parent folder for source and interpretation details.

members.name: GIA Global Bed Topography
members.description: Modelled bed topography from the GIA run identified as mv1e21_fr1e24_w0p0_weakEarth_t20. Values are in metres, with the legend from -1000 m to 1000 m. Record the run identifier when exporting or comparing this layer. Please click the parent folder for source and interpretation details.

members.name: Lowry2024 Ice Sheet Model
members.description: Modelled Antarctic ice thickness at 9.5 ka (9,500 years ago) for run ism_hotf0-0_mv7-5e20_fr1e24. Values are in metres, with the legend from 0 m to 4500 m. Click a point to chart modelled ice thickness through the available time steps, with one line per model run. Please click the parent folder for source and interpretation details.

members.name: PSKRIPS Wind Speed 2017-02-01
members.description: Daily mean wind speed 10 m above the surface on 1 February 2017 from the displayed P-SKRIPS atmospheric output. Values are in metres per second, from 0 m/s (dark purple) to 24 m/s (yellow), and are derived from the U and V components as sqrt(u² + v²). Please click the parent folder for model methods, limitations and citation details.

members.name: PSKRIPS Wind Arrows 2017-02-01
members.description: Daily mean wind 10 m above the surface on 1 February 2017, shown as arrows. Each arrow points in the direction the wind is blowing and is coloured by speed in metres per second. Overlay it on the wind-speed layer or view it independently. Please click the parent folder for model methods, limitations and citation details.

members.name: PSKRIPS Atmosphere Daily Mean in Celsius 2017-02-01
members.description: Daily mean near-surface air temperature on 1 February 2017 from the displayed P-SKRIPS atmospheric output. Values are in degrees Celsius, with the legend from -30 ℃ to 0 ℃. This is the same field as the kelvin layer in different units. Please click the parent folder for model details.

members.name: PSKRIPS Atmosphere Daily Mean in Kelvin 2017-02-01
members.description: Daily mean near-surface air temperature on 1 February 2017 from the displayed P-SKRIPS atmospheric output. Values are in kelvin, with the legend from 243.15 K to 273.15 K. This is the same field as the Celsius layer in different units. Please click the parent folder for model details.

members.name: Tankersley Sediment Thickness 2022
members.description: Estimated thickness of non-magnetic sedimentary cover above magnetic basement beneath the Ross Ice Shelf and Ross Embayment, based on Tankersley et al. (2022). Values are in metres, with the legend from 0 m to 4500 m. This is a geophysical interpretation; consult the source uncertainty grids for quantitative use. Please click the parent folder for methods, access and citation details.

members.name: Ice thickness blocks: band 9, Ross Sea POC
members.description: Experimental 3D columns derived from ice_ds.nc thickness band 9. Thickness is rounded upward into 250 m classes and positioned on the ETOPO surface. Column height is illustrative and does not represent a reconstructed physical ice surface. Please click the parent folder for interpretation and disclaimer information.

catalog.name: Sea ice forecast
catalog.description:
Introduction

This process provides an 8-week forecast of Antarctic sea ice concentration: the fraction of each 1-degree grid cell covered by sea ice, from 0 for open water to 1 for complete ice cover.

Key findings

The graph neural network developed by Tobias Milz, Varvara Vetrova and Marwan Katurji had the lowest error on three of four sea-ice-concentration measures in the study benchmark. Sea-surface temperature was identified as the main source of forecast skill beyond the seasonal climatology.

Forecast provided

One map is available for each of the next eight weeks. Concentration is displayed as a percentage, cells below 1% are left clear, and a new forecast is generated each Monday. Open the process below, select a week and run it; click the resulting map to chart all eight forecast weeks at a location.

Data and model setup

The model uses the previous four weeks of conditions. Sea ice concentration comes from NSIDC-0051, produced from DMSP passive-microwave satellite observations and distributed by the National Snow and Ice Data Center. Atmospheric and ocean predictors come from ERA5, produced by the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts and distributed through the Copernicus Climate Data Store. Predictors include 10 m wind, 2 m air temperature, mean sea-level pressure, sea-surface temperature and total precipitation.

Contributions and data ownership

  • Forecast model and study: Tobias Milz, Varvara Vetrova and Marwan Katurji, University of Canterbury. Tobias Milz prepared the manuscript and figures; all authors reviewed the manuscript.
  • Sea ice observations: NSIDC-0051 is produced from DMSP passive-microwave observations and distributed by NSIDC. NSIDC and the source-data providers retain stewardship of the observation product.
  • Environmental predictors: ERA5 is produced by ECMWF and distributed by the Copernicus Climate Data Store. ECMWF/Copernicus terms continue to apply.
  • Research support: New Zealand Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment through the TAIAO programme, and the Antarctic Science Platform.
  • Ownership: The dashboard does not transfer ownership of NSIDC, ERA5 or other upstream data. Each source remains subject to its provider’s citation and licence terms.

Model limitations

  1. The forecast is deterministic and does not provide an uncertainty range.
  2. The 1-degree grid does not resolve narrow leads or small coastal features.
  3. It forecasts concentration only, not ice thickness, drift or navigational safety.
  4. Forecast skill generally decreases with lead time.
  5. The pole hole is displayed as zero and must not be interpreted as observed open water.

Study and research data

Milz, T., Vetrova, V. and Katurji, M. (2026), Graph neural networks for Antarctic sea ice concentration forecasting, Scientific Reports: https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-026-70984-7. The preprocessed research data are available from the SICGraph data repository.

Contact

Forecast product and technical contact: Tobias Milz, School of Earth and Environment, University of Canterbury. Email: tobi.milz@canterbury.ac.nz.

Disclaimer

This forecast is provided for scientific exploration and informational use. It is supplied "as is" and must not be used as the sole basis for navigation, field safety or other safety-critical decisions.
